utterances.text: Well, if that's what you counted, it's seven. You listed them correctly. Major, Colonel, and Lieutenant-Colonel, I became during the war. I started the war as the Captain -- as Captain 1st Class.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We have 1991, you were Captain first class; December of 1995, you ended up with the rank of Colonel. Do you know of any one soldier in the VRS or JNA that was able so quickly to achieve seven ranks over a course of 13 years?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know some who started with the rank of Major. I know some who started with the rank of Captain. I know many who skipped quite a few ranks and went to a very high rank. There were also other officers who had such a speedy promotion line as I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, on June 28th, 1997, you became Major-General in the VRS; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Up until --

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1997. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Up to what point, sir. How long did you stay as a Major-General in the VRS, from June 28th, 1997 to what date?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed as a Major-General in the VRS, and I think my rank was verified in the Yugoslav army in 2001 which, according to the Yugoslav rules I stayed Colonel for six years.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I followed that entirely and it isn't really a major point, but maybe we should just clarify. If you became Colonel in December of 1995, then you became Major-General a year and a half later, June 28th, 1997, I'm not sure if we got it translated properly, you said that you had to stay to be a Colonel for - I forget what you say - four years or so? Six years. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1995, I acquired the rank of Colonel both in the VRS and the Yugoslav Army. I became Major-General in the VRS in 199, and in the Yugoslav Army in 2001, so for six years I was a Colonel in the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that. It helps with my time-line. So in 1999 when you met with Obrenovic, what position or positions did you have with respect to both the VRS and the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I was not assigned to any duty at the time or whether I was the head of the centre for military strategic research. It could be either.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Help me understand this better. These two staffs that were known at the time for a brief period of time. One was called the "djeneralnista," and the other one was called the "generalnista"; do you remember that or know anything about that? I know I mispronounced it, forgive me?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no two staffs. There was a Main Staff during the war; however, it was renamed General Staff in peacetime. It had to be the Supreme Command or the General Staff during the war as well as, as I understand things.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What I want to know is did you sit on that staff, which ever name it was on, in 1999?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a member of the Main Staff in 1996 and a member of the General Staff in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who in 1999 was the assistant commander for intelligence and security at the time that you were there, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a single function. When the General Staff was set up, there was security administration that had its head, and there was intelligence administration separate from it; and it was subordinate either to the chief or the chief of the staff sector, I'm not sure which.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What are their names? Who are these people?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of the security administration was Mr. Milomir Savcic, and the head of the intelligence administration was Colonel, a man with moustache, dark hair; but I will remember his name later during this trial, I promise you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm really just interested in Mr. Savcic for the moment and leading up to it. He's also what you described, and I think your counsel has used the word, he's your "kum," your best man or best friend, if you want to translate it strictly?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not my "kum" at the time. We finished academy together and we saw each other during the war only at the front. We became "kums" only later.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you at any time including the tenure that you sat on the staff with him, did you ever share with him the events of July 1995 and the purported conversations that you claim you had with Mr. Obrenovic on the 16th and 17th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some suspicions and suppositions that there was an indictment against him. However, we only discussed general topics we never discussed any details relating to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about Mr. Zivanovic. I note that he attended the meeting with the OTP in 2001 with you. Did you ever share with, I think it's Mr. Milenko Zivanovic, the contents of this purported conversation you had with Obrenovic on the 16th and 17th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not this conversation, nor any other conversation, nor any detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Help me with this: Did you know if Mr. Zivanovic at any time met with the Krstic defence team?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned about this by reviewing materials during this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. We're going to switch gears again. I'm just telling you, so you know where I'm going, so it doesn't come as a surprise, which I'm sure it won't. I want to talk a little bit about the time that you spent in Visegrad, if you will. Now, at the time, you referenced or mentioned that you were a commander of a battalion sent to Visegrad from March through June of 1992 and then again from April 1st, 1992 to May 18th, 1992, and that's just so the record, everyone has it, it's on page 30675 and 30676 of your prior testimony. Then there was a question put to you by your counsel and that appears on page 30676, it goes like this: "Q. How did events develop in Visegrad while you were there?" Answer, and you quote among other things: "Peace and order had been established." What I'm curious to know, sir, that is it true that peace and order was established there because you as the commander of a battalion were involved and working with the political leadership, the SDS, and all other top officials in Visegrad and were determined to engage in an effective combat; and thanks to that, you were able to succeed and bring peace and order in Visegrad? So it wasn't just the military, it was your cooperation with the civilians, would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to give you an elaborate answer to match your question. There is some mix-up with the months April, May, June, et cetera. I arrived or rather was sent to the area of Visegrad in mid-April 1992 on the 12th or 13th of April as a member of the still-existing JNA as a commander of the battalion of the mountain brigade of the Uzice Corps. My task was to lift the blockade of the hydro-electric power plant in Visegrad and the storage house in Visegrad as well. The entire brigade was engaged in this in addition to another two battalions and some support units. We carried out our mission successfully. Order and peace were restored in Visegrad. Before that, the Serbs had been expelled from the town. Later, they came back and while the JNA was in the area of Visegrad including myself, that is until the 18th of May, over 95 percent of the residents of Visegrad were -- came back and lived together. So I don't take all the credit for that. I was just one of the participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what I really was interested in and thank you for that detailed answer, was did you also find it important to be coordinating and cooperating with the SDS and the political leadership there as well as the top officials in Visegrad in order to accomplish this?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One has to cooperate with the authorities, either at the level of a republic or the local level. I didn't organise elections nor had I any input in the make-up of this authority. Whether these authorities were made up of members of the SDS or any other political party was totally irrelevant to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, how important was it for you at that time to maintain good relations with that entire political leadership, the SDS, and other top officials in Visegrad while you were commander of that battalion, meaning the civilians, how important was it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was with the JNA, I had no contacts with them at all. I had contacts with my brigade commander and whether he had contacts with them, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's take a look again at that interview you gave, 2D638, if you don't mind. And it would be on -- I'm sorry, page 13 in English and page 16, I believe, in B/C/S. Sir, it's on the first part in the English when it has -- where it has your initials VP, and it's the latter part of that paragraph that I wanted to just briefly discuss with you because it relates to 1995, your cooperation with the civilians based on other questions just so you know. It says here: "We formed that brigade and we had enough equipment, ammunition, all the potential, but most importantly, the entire political leadership, the SDS, and all other top officials in Visegrad were determined to engage in effective combat, and thanks to that, we succeeded." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen that. This refers to a different period, that is when the JNA withdrew and when I went back to Visegrad and became commander of the Visegrad Brigade that had been formed at that time. It is only natural to make such a statement during war that can certain -- can have certain impact on people to defend themselves because it was war. These speeches made during war do not have a long life. As I see it, I had to cooperate with everyone on whom I depended in organising armed defence. I couldn't do that on my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you also implement the spirit of cooperation with the civilians and probably the SDS in July of 1995 when you were in the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to establish cooperation under the same basis as I did in Visegrad, however, not all people are the same. I didn't meet with understanding and the cooperation was not as nearly good as it was in Visegrad and not as good as I had expected it to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll move away from Visegrad. Let's talk about the liberation of Glodjansko Brdo. Maybe I should just spell it so I don't have to later. It's G-l-o-z-d-a-n-s-k-o [sic]; are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When was it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in February 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And where is Glodjansko Brdo if you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is 15 kilometres or thereabout south of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just because some of these names -- how far is it from Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could be 25 or 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Kilometres?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Because we've had witnesses tell us it's X amount as the crow flies so I just didn't know exactly what you meant. Now where is Glodi, G-l-o-d-i?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Glodi is a village south of Glodjansko Brdo on the slopes of the Glodjansko Brdo and close to the River Drinjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, at that time, the liberation of Glodjansko Brdo, and again it's in the article, and we'll come to it in a second, you identified after that liberation that it was a powerful stimulus and inspiration to all citizens, soldiers, and residents of Zvornik municipality and the broader area to later move forward more resoundingly; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember. As people say, nothing succeeds like success. If you achieve success in combat, it will be motivation for new successes. Before that, dozens of civilians and soldiers went missing, their families knew nothing about them. Zvornik was under threat, the economy was in distress. Some soldiers had been demobilised, and the front line had been shortened; so once the success was achieved, it affected the whole morale of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I was really interested more of the civilians and the residents, but at that time, what was your purported zone of defence? Was it as limited as it was in July of 1995 or did it cover the entire Zvornik municipality?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have to make distinction between two notions that you disagreed at the very beginning. The Zvornik Brigade has an area of responsibility for conducting combat activities. It was beyond the borders of Zvornik municipality. Within this zone of responsibility for conducting combat operations, a brigade had a fortified the zone of defence which is a piece of territory in which units of the Zvornik Brigade were deployed. In other words, and for better understanding, wherever there were soldiers, that was the area that I was responsible for.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What about where there was civilians or population, the residents of Zvornik. You weren't responsible to protect that? Again we're talking still about February of 1993, and we'll get to July 1995 in a short time.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilian population and the town of Zvornik could be protected by defending the territory. And it is precisely this defence zone was the territory from which we defended the town of Zvornik and its population behind the frontlines. I had no other responsibility with regards to the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you also insists that the area of responsibility of the brigade does not cover just the borders of a municipality but went behind, beyond - I'm sorry - did you insist on that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't me who insisted on that. That is what we received from the corps. You could see in the map that it stretches over the front line into the territory controlled by the 2nd Corps of the BiH Army, so if you consider me responsible for that as well, I can't help it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not here to hold anybody responsible for anything, sir. Let's take a look at your interview on page 14 in English and it's page 17 in B/C/S. I'll read it because I'm not sure where it is in the B/C/S, but I'm sure you'll find it and please if you need more time, just tell us. This is again the first full paragraph where the journalist asks you a question and then you respond with your initials VP and you state in the latter portion of that exchange: "I also insisted that the area of responsibility of the brigade did not cover just the borders of a municipality but went beyond." You go on, but for right now I'd like to focus on that. I can give the page number again, it's page 14 in English and page 17 in B/C/S. I'm sorry if I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see that page. Can I have it, please, on my screen in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll see if I can get you a hard copy, if I marked it properly. There's markings just highlighted on the B/C/S, but I'm sure --

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Now, did this zone of responsibility, whether or not you insisted on it, it doesn't matter that much, did that change at any time from 1993 up until July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at this sentence which ends "... the zone of the brigade," without specifying either defence or responsibility stretches beyond the board borders of the municipality; what I meant by this is, what I meant is that one cannot successfully defend Zvornik if you do it from your doorstep. You have to push the enemy a little further on in order to make the defence effective and efficient. As for the second part of your question, the zone of responsibility for conducting combat operations of the Zvornik Brigade assigned to it in 1992, I believe remained throughout the whole war, but the defence zone did change, however. I mean the area where the Zvornik Brigade was deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'll address that but first you say here on line 23, "You have to push the enemy a little bit further on," in fact you want to push them as far away as possible, don't you? Not a little further, far, far away.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the point of fighting is to push the enemy, to fight the enemy. That's the essence of a war. An armed conflict is the core of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, sir, did your zone of responsibility or zone of defence, as you defined it in the maps, and we'll take a look at those again tomorrow, did that change at any time from the time you first came to Zvornik on the 18th of December all the way through July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just told you, Mr. Ostojic. You are hearing me both in the Serbian and in English. The zone of responsibility for conducting combat activities did not change. What does that mean? If a Muslim group had infiltrated the town of Zvornik, I would have to fight it first because that was my obligation and duty. However, it does not make me the mayor of Zvornik. Just like the 28th Division appeared, once they crossed the Drinjaca and Glode and entered the zone of responsibility of combat activities of the Zvornik Brigade, the Zvornik Brigade engaged in combat with it. That was the responsibility of the brigade to engage in armed fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm confident you weren't the mayor of Zvornik, but what about if it was infiltrated in July of 1995, let's say, with POWs. What role does the Zvornik Brigade have?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by the group of POWs infiltrating the area. Can you be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's take away the word or the "POW," and let's just say if there were Muslim forces that infiltrated the Zvornik Brigade at some schools, regardless of what their identity was, meaning whether they were POWs, civilians, or military, does the Zvornik Brigade get involved in that at all?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hold your horses, this is not exactly how it is. We cannot mix up infiltration by groups, civilians, and prisoners of war. If anyone captured prisoners of war, they knew exactly where they were taking them, and they knew whether they were exposed to any risk. Since the Zvornik Brigade wasn't ordered to receive POWs, and they were accommodated in the area of Zvornik does not necessarily impose any obligation on the Zvornik Brigade. It is the duty and the obligation of those who brought them into the area and not the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I know that's your position, and I would beg to differ with you. Do you know whether or not the Drina Corps, Mr. Milenko Zivanovic or General Krstic ever informed the Zvornik Brigade while you were commander or when you were away on this tactical group mission to actually capture the Muslims who were trying to flee through the area near or around Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have seen here thousands of documents and heard many testimonies, and we all know how these events evolved. We never heard that either General Zivanovic or Krstic ordered either Obrenovic or me to receive the POWs, provide them with accommodation, or anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, it might have got translated a little awkwardly, but not to receive them, but did they give you instruction to capture enemy Muslims who were trying to get across to their territory?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can show the order dated the 13th to prevent the break through of Muslim forces from Srebrenica to Tuzla, that's what this order contains.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Does it contain the word "capture," that it was the responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade to capture them?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those who were not taken prisoner already, not those who had already been taken prisoner because it would be tantamount to retaking them prisoner, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's the way you defined it, that it's a capture or a retaking or whatever way; but you got specific instructions, did you not, from Krstic on the 15th of July, 1995, to capture Bosnian Muslims, did you not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I really don't want to interrupt, but it may well be that this line of examination is based upon a mistake in the transcript. I'm told that at line 55 or page 55, line 14, what the witness actually said is the one who brought the prisoners not the one who captured the prisoners. Perhaps that ought to be checked because that's the whole premise of this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pandurevic, perhaps you can clarify that for us. Mr. Haynes is referring to the part of the transcript where you were answering the question and you told Mr. Ostojic: "Hold your horses, this is not exactly how it is. We cannot mix up infiltration by groups to civilians and prisoners of war. If anyone captured prisoners of war ..." this is what is submitted to being wrong. Did you say if anyone captured prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, I said if anyone brought them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Does that change your situation, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll deal with it. Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll just stick with this unique distinction you make between zone of defence and zone of responsibility. What I thought and I got from your testimony in direct on the 27th of January 2009, you said: "Defend all inhabited places and the town of Zvornik at all costs." And this is on page 30697 and it related to Exhibit P280 and the time period was January of 1993 that you made this statement. Quote, again I'll just -- for your benefit: "Defend [Realtime transcript read in error, "depend"] all inhabited places and the town of Zvornik at all costs." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't, but it's true, it was recorded those were my words and that was my task, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That was in June of 1993. My question really is: When did the mission or the goal of the Zvornik Brigade change to simply be this limited zone of defence that you claim was solely and exclusively under your command in July of 1995 from that which it was in 1993 basically to: "Defend all inhabited places and the town of Zvornik at all costs." When did it change?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no change. In 1995, in Memici, at Pandurica, at Baljkovica, Boskovici, and everywhere else, we defended each village and town in the Zvornik area from those positions. I couldn't defend Zvornik from a residential building. I defended Zvornik at a distance of 20 or 30 kilometres from Zvornik itself. It wasn't my task to protect a single school building from having POWs accommodated there if that is what you mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, it's time for a break, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, I was just told on page 57 line 24, the word "depend" was used, but I think it should be "defend." I don't know if it was his answer or my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have a 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pandurevic, we're going to address some other issues and maybe come back to some of these themes, hopefully. I'd like now to discuss briefly the civilians in Zvornik, really the population as a whole and who lived there in 1995, et cetera; but first you mentioned, I think yesterday, of a person by the name of Misko Vasic; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How, if at all, is he related to Colonel Vasic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think no relation at all, as far as I know. The family name is the same. He came from Zivinice municipality, Dragomir Vasic and Misko Vasic, I think, was a loca from Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And Colonel Vasic, would that be Dragomir Vasic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Dragomir Vasic is a Colonel, but whether we both mean Colonel Dragomir Vasic, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's what I was referring to, that's why I just wanted to clarify that. Where was he a colonel, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And at what period of time?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was demobilised from the army and appointed chief of the security services centre in Zvornik, when the introduction of ranks occurred in the MUP, I don't know. I heard something about that during this trial. I think he turned up with that rank sometime late in 1995. As you see first rank and a colonel immediately. I myself wasn't nearly that good.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I want to discuss the influence of the civilian authorities in Zvornik in July of 1995, in particular, but if you can demark for us when the influence in Zvornik by the civilians started, feel free to do so. When you talk about the influence that the civilian authorities had over the brigade, when did that commence?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the influence existed from the time it was first set up, simply because the municipal authorities were involved in the setting up of the TO units which later evolved and became the brigade. Their influence was indirect because a lot of the logistics and the supplies required for the work of the brigade came from the ranks of the local community. It was for that very reason that the local authorities believed they had every right to interfere with the command processes as well, simply because they were providing some of the supplies that were used for the brigade to be able to get on with its life and work.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you agree or disagree with this right to interfere with the command processes, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to remain in keeping with the procedure of command from the very top, the commander down to the lowest-ranking unit. If you look at that hierarchy, if you look at the chain of command, I don't think you are likely to come across municipal bodies anywhere in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So just so I fully understand you, I take it you did not agree with their impression or what they thought was their right; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to commanding the brigade, yes, I disagreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about the influence it may have had over the brigade? Do you think they should have any influence over a brigade or the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were a number of ways for them to exercise influence over the brigade. They viewed me as an outsider because I was no local. That's how they saw me. As for the relationship between the municipal authorities and the brigade members there used to be various kinds of links and interested involved through the local communes and all the way up to the municipality itself; then there was party line, the political line, the local economy, and a number of other ways as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We know the political party there was the SDS in 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true they were in power but there were other parties around as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Help me understand this. This influence that the civilian authorities had on the Zvornik Brigade, did it continue to maintain throughout the period that you were there meaning from 1993 or if you will, the 18th of December, 1992, all the way through and after July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the influence continued throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, in some of your testimony you referenced "senior officer." Would Colonel Vasic fit in your definition of a senior officer?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an officer of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Help me understand some of the personal difficulties you had with the civilian, civilians in Zvornik in 1995 and if necessary, you can share with us from 1993 when you first got there.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be perfectly clear and accurate, I myself had no problems with the civilians in Zvornik whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's take a look at 2D646 again which is your 65 ter summary, and we can just stay on the first page which is 13. And it's the first bullet point -- I mean the fifth bullet point, I'm sorry under the description of the summary of your testimony. I don't know if it's up -- here it comes. I'll read it for you because I apologise for not having it in B/C/S. The fifth bullet point. It says: "He," meaning you, Mr. Pandurevic "will describe the influence enjoyed by the civilian authorities over the brigade and his own personal difficulties with the local civilian authorities." So really I just want to, because I don't know that you covered it much in your direct other than when you mentioned Brano Grujic, but we'll get to him in a few minutes, I just want to generally know what personal difficulties did you have with the civilians and specifically - I apologise if it's a compound question - with whom and when?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may be an interpretation issue. What I see mentioned here is relations to the municipal civilian authorities and not civilians as such, by which I mean the locals, and I didn't have any problems with the locals. That's what I meant when I answered your question. When I say that I was facing some difficulties with the municipal political authorities, the local authorities, those weren't problems in the sense of an ongoing and interrupted conflict. There were situations where misunderstandings occurred depending on some situations that needed dealing with, situations of general interest and of interest to the brigade specifically. I was in touch with the municipal president, the president of the executive board, and through them with certain local company managers.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And when was that that you had those personal difficulties with the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Soon after my arrival, the military situation in the Zvornik area was what it was. The town was facing direct threat. A lot of the civilian population such as women and children would leave the Zvornik area over night to go to Serbia. There were certain problems involving mobilisation, bringing up manpower levels in the brigade, organising the brigade in the proper way. There were thousands of civilians in the brigade and very few soldiers, if you understand what I mean. I tried to work with the corps command and the appropriate bodies of the defence ministry in order to try and resolve those issues. I did not always meet with much understanding on the part of those bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to influence by the civilian authorities over the brigade. Did that influence that the civilian authorities had over the Zvornik Brigade exist in July of 1995 as well?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that those influences existed throughout the war. I cannot remember exactly what kind of influences were there in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, specifically from whom, meaning which civilian authorities, had this influence in the Zvornik Brigade from the time that you were there up through December 1995, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I told you, that was the president of the municipality, the chairman of the executive committee, some members of the executive committee. I had soldiers on the front without boots. They were only wearing trainers. I asked them for money to purchase boots but they didn't understand my request or they bought some cardboard boots that disintegrated after the first rain, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm just -- I know that might be personal difficulties. I'm trying to focus now for the time being on the influence those civilian authorities had. I know you gave me their title, but give me their names if you would be kind enough, who were these people who had influence on your brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a time, Brano Grujic was the president of the municipality. He was succeeded by Jovan Mitrovic, the chairman of the executive committee were Dragan Spasojevic, Zoran Zekic a certain Budim Acimovic and many others. They changed frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, maybe it's my fault, but I just want to know of the people who had influence, civilian authorities who had influence on the Zvornik Brigade. I want to know who those people are, and I know some of them may be included in that. Is that all the people who had influence in the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in a certain way, and indirectly. If they go to their native village and talk to the soldiers who are mobilised from that village and then they tell you, We are giving you everything that your commander is asking for and he doesn't give that to you, they created a rift between the commander and the soldiers by spreading this kind of rumours and hearsay. That was one form of influence. Another form was, look, Pandurevic is sending you outside of Zvornik to give your life for someone else. They would assemble these soldiers, talk to them, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And now, you yourself stated in your testimony at page 30703 while describing this one exhibit 7D1001 at the commencement of your tenure at Zvornik approximately March of 1993, I think was the issue, you said the following: "Soldiers and officers" and I have, in parentheses, of Zvornik Brigade, end parentheses, have demonstrated a considerable amount of wilfulness and also the desire to lead on the basis of their own decisions." Do you remember that testimony roughly?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember speaking about their self-management way of thinking and acting in which a platoon commander or a company commander was turned into a courier after talking to soldiers. Before I issue an order, they would come, this is -- and say this is not what the soldiers want, they have some other ideas and suggestions. Let me just give you one example. When it comes to carrying out tasks in the place where you live, they were ready to carry out any task. When I had to divide the battalion into two sections and confine one half of the battalion into undefended area, 100 percent of them came to the area in the morning because they thought that whoever came first, they would remain there. If I order them to leave the area, I don't believe that they would gladly do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When, if at all, to the best of your recollection, did this "self-management" end?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This had never been -- has never been uprooted altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And really, what you're saying, I think, in the quote, and you correct me if I am wrong, is that some soldiers and officers, as you have identified, in that brigade from time to time wouldn't even follow your orders, and they would do things independently with no regard to the course of action that you may envision; would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My orders did not apply to one soldier only. My orders referred to the unit and it was important to me for the unit to carry out its task. There would always be soldiers who would either fail to disappear or will fail to carry out the task or would rather choose the task that they think they could perform best.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well you identified some officers in that sentence that I quoted from your testimony. What officers were those that kind of had this self-management style and made their own decisions, as you identified? Or led on the basis of their own decisions? Which officers were those of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each officer or unit commander has an inherent right to issue orders, it does not have to amount to wilfulness if it is in the spirit of general rules and regulations. But there were those who didn't have any rank or any military training who were holding positions of command. Such individuals were always prepared to protect their "unit" and their position instead of carrying out my orders and leaving their place of residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me just go back to the quote: "Soldiers and officers have demonstrated a considerable amount of wilfulness and also the desire to lead on the basis of their own decisions." Please identify which officers you were referring to of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you names. There were over 50 company commanders, there were 12 or 13 battalion commanders, and there were huge differences among them. Some of them were very conscientious and responsible and skilled, some of them weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And this continued on throughout your tenure at Zvornik Brigade, correct, all wait through, I think, December 1995 or thereabouts; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, only it wasn't so prominent in 1995 as it was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm going to come back to this topic, just I had a thought. When was your meeting with Morillon that you escorted him back and forth, what year was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I wasn't sure if it was 1994 or 1993. Now, sticking with this civilian authorities theme, if you will, what was your relationship like with the MUP of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Official.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you describe it for me?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would meet Mr. Vasic occasionally at meetings in the municipality hall or at the assembly meeting. If it was necessary for the MUP and the army to be engaged somewhere, we would discuss that, although it happened very seldom. They had their own chain of command. We cooperated in the sense if it happened that soldiers were -- left the front line with weapons and caused some troubles we would address these problems together; however, we didn't have any other joint operations or obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Was there, in your opinion, cooperation and a joint operation in July of 1995 with the Zvornik MUP?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One unit of the Zvornik MUP, one PJP company commanded by Mr. Borovcanin in July 1995, was under my command through Borovcanin in the fighting at Baljkovica, I think until the 18th of July. I know that in June, they took part in the defence of the Vis feature in the area of the Sekovac [as interpreted] Brigade where one of my units also took part under the command of Colonel Andric.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just focus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could get the Sekovici Brigade is what we meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In the transcript as you see it says Sekovac but you said what, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The brigade from Sekovici or the 1st Birac Infantry Brigade that's its proper name.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And taking aside the one PJP company that you mentioned in July of 1995, what was the other units or MUP members doing in July of 1995, was there any cooperation or assistance that they were providing in -- during the war when the Muslims were trekking from Srebrenica through Zvornik to Kladanj or Tuzla; do you know?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About their engagement in the general area of the public security centre of Zvornik until July the 15th, I knew nothing; however, as of the 15th, I know that they were searching the terrain, the area of Snagovo, Crni Vrh, and the asphalt road. I remember that some time after the 20th or the 24th, we saw in one of the reports, I requested through the corps command for a coordinated cooperation to be established with the MUP because we were doing things independently.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so I'm clear, but before the 24th, there was no coordination or cooperation with the MUP authorities with the exception of the one that you mentioned already; correct? In July, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that in July, at the level of the public security centre of Zvornik, there was the police forces staff commanded by Vasic, and he was in command of all the MUP forces deployed in the area at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then we'll come back to this topic, there are several documents that I'm confident that you've already seen through other witnesses of Mr. Vasic, and we'll go over that possibly tomorrow. I want to go back to the civilian authorities of Zvornik. You stated or page 30983 when you testified that you were not on good terms with Brano Grujic, can you describe that? Why and -- why were you not on good terms with him?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While he was the president of the municipality, we had to maintain an official relationship, whether we liked each other or not. That was in the interest of the brigade and the defence of Zvornik itself. We were not on friendly terms. We did not visit each other. There was -- were lots of misunderstanding on his part with regards to my request. Therefore, the relationship was rather tense when it came to finding solutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. What about your relationship with Colonel Dragomir Vasic of the MUP, can you describe that for us?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a period of time after I came to Zvornik, he was a company commander in the brigade. My plan was to appoint him assistant for morale in the battalion; however, a request for his demobilisation arrived, and he was subsequently demobilised and became the head of the security centre in Zvornik. We were not friends. We did not socialise. We did not visit each other. I did not know his family. We just maintained an official relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did Colonel Dragomir Vasic have any influence over the soldiers and officers of the Zvornik Brigade at any time when he was with MUP and not specifically with the brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The MUP as an institution had no influence on the brigade. Vasic had a certain influence on some of the soldiers from a company from the 6th Battalion who were refugees from his village. He supplied some relief and assistance to their families, but he never interfered with the command of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, this 6th Battalion, that's at the time in July, that was when Ostoja Stanisic was the commander and his deputy was Marko Milosevic; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just ask you briefly about Milos Stupar, what was the relationship between you and Milos Stupar at the time that you were at the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that man maybe twice in my life, and I can't tell you anything about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so we know who we're talking about, ones of the times was in July -- on July 15th, 1995 when you came back to the Zvornik command; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I believe I saw him once before that at a celebration in Sekovici, the anniversary of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I appreciate that. Let me just quickly turn to a couple of documents I want to introduce, and then we can talk about it in a little greater detail tomorrow. First, if we can have P117 please. We'll spend some time talking about POWs and the orders that you may have received tomorrow, but I just want to bring this one to your attention now. I'm looking -- I don't know if it's up yet, Mr. Pandurevic, but it should are shortly and just so I give you background on it, it's dated July 13th, 1995. It's from the command of the Drina Corps, and it seems to be signed or at least a block signature from Major-General Milenko Zivanovic. When you've had a chance to look at it would you please tell me and I'll put some questions to you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm everything you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of this order in July of 1995 on or about the 15th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about this order on the 13th. I arrived at Zvornik on the 15th with the order of General Krstic and with the task similar to those stated here and that is to block and to destroy the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I notice that your testimony, even on direct you always talk about block and destroy, but does it at all mention capture?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the same notion. We took prisoners after and during the fighting and during the search of the terrain. Of those soldiers were the prisoners under the jurisdiction of the Zvornik Brigade, they were put up in the military remand prison in the Standard barracks, and the Zvornik Brigade was responsible for those prisoners. Unfortunately, with regard to the overall number of the casualties, those were the only ones who survived including a small number of the ones that survived from the execution sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get to that a little bit. Thank you for that. But if you look at paragraph which is numbered 3, after the declaration of "I hereby order," Major-General Zivanovic seems to be using the past tense saying: "Put captured and disarmed Muslims in suitable buildings that can be secured by small forces and immediately inform the superior command." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are you telling us that Mr. Zivanovic was ordering you guys to use suitable buildings, but you would only use one building for potential or captured disarmed Muslims?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I did not act on this order. This item was copied for the most part from the order that came from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, regardless of whether it was copied or not from an order from the Main Staff, the instruction, and I realise you weren't there on the 13th, but when you came back on the 15th, did Obrenovic or anybody else give you this and tell you, we got specific instructions on the 13th of July from Major-General Zivanovic, X, Y, and Z; did they discuss it with you at any time?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because this order refers to certain forces that were not nearly as those that Dragan Obrenovic knew when he reported to me on the 15th and by that time, this order became pointless.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So then let's just quickly, since we're on the topic and have some time, look at 7D686, please. And we have both actually. This is an order, sir, as it's coming up and you see it that you've given evidence on. It's dated the 15th of July, 1995, from now Major-General Radislav Krstic and did you receive this order prior to returning to the Zvornik Brigade command on the 15th of July, 1995 at approximately noon, I think is just testimony? Did you receive that order prior to you coming to the command?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received this order orally from General Krstic at the Krivace IKM, and it was encrypted and forwarded to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And it was forwarded as we can see at approximately 1041 by the little box on the right-hand side; do you see that? And then in handwritten form on the outside box it says either 10.00 C, which I think is time or "casova" [phoen] or approximately 10.41; would that be about right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says, at 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In this order, the first paragraph, doesn't General Krstic also tell you to capture Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well your testimony in essence was that when you got there, your assignment was to block and destroy the enemy Muslim forces. How do you reconcile that if he told you you should take measures to block, break-up, and capture Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well more or less that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now just looking at the second paragraph, and we'll come to it a little later, because of your zone of defence that you need distinction with the zone of responsibility. In the second paragraph of the order, do you see what I call kind of an expansion, if we accept your zone of defence theory, an expansion of your zone if he says here, in order to protect the population and material goods, are you going beyond the borders that you described for us when you had the map behind you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, you had to act at the place where the enemy appeared, and I had to engage in fighting with them. This all happened within the boundaries of the zone for conducting combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to briefly introduce this document so we can touch on it and that's P1172, and it's an intercept that was purportedly captured with you, sir, on it and you can clarify that for us if you disagree. I'm just curious about a couple of things there, and really I'm going to focus your attention but you obviously have the right, and you can look at the whole thing, I really want to focus on the second or the latter third portion of this intercept where apparently you with either Milosevic or Mijatovic are having an exchange. And again, sir, I don't know if it's you, but that's what the Prosecution is alleging, and this is again it's just for the record is the 15th of July, 1995, at 0855 hours.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I took part in this conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I just want and I'm curious, we'll get back to this, I'm curious in this line where you talk about: "When is that information from?" The answer is: "This morning." Then you respond: "This morning. And when was the dawn? Give me an overview now, brother." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to this part when it says what the situation is, where did you find this word "svanolo" [phoen] or the dawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm reading it from the English translation.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you give me the beginning of the line where you started reading from?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sure: "P: This morning, and when was the dawn? Give me an overview now, brother." It's really a minor point but I'm just -- haven't really asked a question yet just to see if you found it.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look up one line, the person is confirming that the information came that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not really concerned with that right now, actually I haven't put a question to you, I just want to orient you to the exhibit itself.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So what I am asking here is for this information to be verified, the 4th, 6th, and 7th Battalion and when that information came; and he said, This morning, and I said, This morning? At daybreak. Meaning very early that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you're telling him it's basically you wanted up-to-date information, and this is at 8.55 I think as we said, in the morning, and the information perhaps that he was conveying to you was dawn and you wanted some up-to-date information, isn't that basically the essence regardless of what the information is; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably, my collocutor was trying to confirm that the situation was still the same at the time of my call as it had been that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You strike me, sir, from listening to your testimony these past few weeks and looking at this intercept by way of one example that you were the type of commander or officer who wanted to see things for himself. For example, like going immediately to the IKM, the forward command post, on the 15th of July, 1995 to see for yourself the size of the enemy column, to see for yourself the strength of the enemy column, and to see for yourself, among other things, the specific whereabouts of the enemy column. Would I be correct? Is that the type of officer you were, and commander?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Talking about my specific problem, my focus was the 28th Division and I went there to see for myself what all of this was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In fact, sir, you didn't, as a commander then -- you didn't rely on secondhand information or information from a tertiary source, did you? You went and wanted to see for yourself what the problem was, what your options may be and how best to address them; would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was sent back there with a specific mission. There was no way I could remain at the Zvornik command and exercise command from the barracks.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the last part of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I went straight to the IKM.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it okay now, in other words, or not? You need to repeat your answer, particularly because the interpreters didn't get the last part of it. What we have here: "Well, I was sent back there with a specific mission. There was no way I could remain at the Zvornik command and exercise command from the barracks." How did you finish your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, by way of illustration of the degree of failure that would have been involved in me trying to exercise command from there, I said it would have been tantamount to Mr. Ostojic cross-examining me from the corridor and not from behind a lectern. I do apologise for the comparison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, would you agree with me that a commander and officer such as yourself relying on secondary or tertiary information is unreasonable? And that's why you, in fact, in this instance, although I'm not particularly talking about your activities on the 15th yet but that's why you went to see for yourself, you went to be able to digest the information yourself; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The best situation is if you get your information in real time. That's what the forces of NATO can afford to have today, but the VRS commanders could in no way obtain that. I had information on my own location that was all the firsthand information I had. All the other information that came from elsewhere was necessarily secondhand information hearsay or information from my associate's assistants and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm going to get to that. I don't think it was just secondhand. I think it was actually fourth removed when you talk about some of the things that people like Obrenovic allegedly told you. So maybe we could address it now. I just want to find out from you, do you agree with me that it's unreasonable to rely on second or thirdhand information or information that is even more so remotely conveyed; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you have no other choice you rely on the information that you have. I received information from my associates and the procedure for obtaining this information was the usual one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not criticising you about that at all, sir. And I understand the situation. Let's talk about some of these people that Obrenovic purportedly told you certain things and let's take, for example, the first one, Dragan Jokic. You said on page 30951 on the 2nd of February, 2009, lines 9 through 11, sorry: "I knew him well. I knew that he was a man who was faced by complicated situations and he is not able to convey the real picture of events." Do you remember giving that testimony approximately?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was in reference to the combat situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When -- I still don't understand. What do you mean he was faced by complicated situations?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he faces a situation like that, Jokic cannot find an appropriate solution. This newly arisen complicated situation overpowers him as opposed to him taking control of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's -- and we'll get back to it more specifically. Let's talk about the late Ljubo Bojanovic for a second. On page 31587 from yesterday, I think, you mentioned that he was an elderly man who had a drink occasionally or all that. Was he a reliable source of information?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when he was in his right state of mind, and when, on a specific mission, he could sometimes be reliable, yes. Nevertheless, he was particularly skillful at dodging his duties and commitments.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I like you, sir, would never think of speaking ill of departed, but can you describe for me if he had a drinking problem to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He liked the occasional drink, he wasn't above it as people say. He could hardly control himself in terms of when he chose to have one. I said yesterday or two days ago that I tried to keep him in the command itself and whenever he felt like it, he could just knock on my door. I was there. I would allow him to have a glass just in order to keep tabs on him so as to make sure I knew exactly how much he'd had on that particular day. But sometimes he was off and he would just enjoy himself. I cannot say that he was a notorious alcoholic though.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well let's talk about this firsthand knowledge, secondhand knowledge, et cetera; and I want to talk about three specific areas when it relates to that. That is I want to talk about the POWs, the executions, and the burials. Now you, sir, did not personally see for yourself the POWs; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you, sir, did not see for yourself the executions; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you, sir, yourself, did not see the burials and I just want to be fair to you because I think you mentioned once when you drove back, you may have seen some bodies, I'm not referring to that. I'm talking about the burials that are the heart of the case, I guess; correct? You did not see it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If you came here and testified giving firsthand knowledge, so you don't have any firsthand knowledge of any of those three things; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, none.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, let me just -- I'm sorry, I didn't mean to interrupt you but it's really -- and I don't have a debate about that at all, sir. Now, you received information from a secondhand source, among others, and we'll get through to it, Obrenovic, purportedly. Just so you know, that's a secondhand source, would you agree?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic. You have very good mastery of all these facts that have nothing to do with the essence of the case. You stick to form. I appreciate your approach, but everything that I've been saying and everything that Obrenovic told me, if we take that and compare it to things that have nothing to do with any contact between Obrenovic and me, all this tallies to a large extent and what I mean specifically is the intercepts on the one hand and the duty officers' log book on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, we're going to go through both of those tomorrow; so you'll have your opportunity to give us your opinion and your thoughts on that. Now this secondhand information that you were receiving from Obrenovic, he got that information from one source according to you was Jokic, who you described as being faced by complicated situations and was not able to convey the real picture of events; right? And this information would be considered thirdhand information, would it not?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you categorise this information like that, your viewpoint is probably a legal one concerning the giving of evidence or something like that. A commander receives information in the middle of fighting, depending on the level of command for the most part this could be secondhand, thirdhand, fourthhand, even fifthhand but a commander has no choice but to trust his associates in situations like these. Speaking of Mr. Jokic, nothing is further from my mind than to say that this person is retarded. Of course he's perfectly able to describe a situation that happened in a room 3 by 4 metres big.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, let's leave Mr. Jokic aside. Let's talk about the late Ljubo Bojanovic. You described him here. Do you think that's reliable information that Obrenovic could use to say that here he is as you've described him "an old man who occasionally drank but was not an alcoholic." Do you think that's a reliable source?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It all depends on whether he's sober at this particular point in time. I would much prefer to talk to you about an independent source, something that comes neither from me nor from Obrenovic nor from Jokic, and that is very easy to verify in terms of truthfulness because what we are doing here is spinning around in circles, firsthand, secondhand, Jokic, Bojanovic. I told you how I felt about that and I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I'm not challenging that. I just wanted to highlight the level of knowledge that these people had and the reliability or unreliability of the sources. Let me ask you this, sir: Now, you said at one point that you were surprised by Dragan Obrenovic's plea agreement. You were surprised by his plea agreement because at that time in July of 1995, and soon thereafter, you had no idea that he was involved as he so pled in any of the executions or the capturing POWs or maintaining of the POWs or the burial of the POWs; correct? And when I say maintaining, really housing, I'm sorry, it's getting late for me as well.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I look at his statement of facts, there are very few facts that I come across that have to do with him and his responsibility. There are more things and more facts there that have to do with others. I stand by my position. I don't know what he took as his guiding idea when he reviewed his situation, his role as it was. Only he knows about his real personal involvement in certain things, but from a commander's perspective in terms of his responsibility, receiving and handling prisoners of war, one thing that I fail to understand is what appears to be his understanding of that particular role.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well my point is in essence that based on the information he gave you, and you've seen and read his plea agreement both before and after you were detained and brought here to The Hague, did he lie to you then in July of 1995 when he was telling you other people were involved and he didn't say anything about himself? I mean surely you don't expect that someone would just admit to their guilt and not be guilty. What benefit would that serve?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that he had agreed for Drago Nikolic and another five police officers to be put on that job. Any information he shared with me about the presence of other persons outside the command of the Zvornik Brigade was confirmed by the log book and the intercepts, and that is entirely true. When talking about the other co-indicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You highlighted for us instances when Mr. Bourgon was questioning you when Dragan Obrenovic lied and specifically instances if you recall, I think there were 10 or 11 of them if not more, now what I'm asking you though now given that you know and you've seen and you've reviewed his plea agreement and the statement of facts that he's agreed to and accepted his culpability in the events that transpired in July of 1995. In July of 1995 he obviously either lied to you or misrepresented to you what his involvement was with both let's say the 4th Battalion as well as the 6th Battalion, wouldn't that be a true statement?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you the story that I heard from him. His admission of guilt, his statement of facts is something almost like a net which he spun in such a way as to involve all the other accused in different ways and to different degrees. I don't know what his reason for that might have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sure he was spinning a web to try and get himself out of the reality and -- with his involvement, but all I'm asking you, sir, do you believe him now that he's accepted his responsibility and he's pled guilty to the crimes that occurred at Orahovac, Petkovci, and Pilici or do you dispute that as you sit here today?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the story that he told me at the time, if he believed in his own guilt, if he admitted to it, then there is nothing more for me to think about then, is there?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me just briefly since we have a moment discuss two exhibits if I can. P378 which is, I think, the Zvornik Brigade duty operations officer diary; but it may have come under a different name from time to time, it's from the 12th of February, 1995 through the 3rd of January, 1996, and I believe the Prosecution will assist in providing you with the original. The war diary. Thank you. So with leave of Court, if the usher can assist us so that Mr. Pandurevic can have that. It's P378. Who, sir, when you -- and you've looked at this before, who is in charge of maintaining that book?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the operative log book. It's not the war diary. This is the log book kept by the operations duty officer. You will hardly ever come across anything in this diary that you wouldn't come across in an interpret combat report or regular combat report or the working notebook. This is a document that is normally produced post festum following the dispatch of the regular combat report. It can also be taken down as events unfold simultaneously following any entries that are made to the working log.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I didn't like the words war diary either but in any event, who maintained this book; do you know? I know we have a period that was covered but who maintained that in July of 1995; do you know?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, it was a different man every day. If you look at the signatures, you will realise that. Operations duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have before me the 13th of July 1995, please. Maybe if we could try to get that one up on the e-court as well, the 13th of July. And if you can't find the 13th, maybe you could try and find the 14th for me, Mr. Pandurevic, and also with the court's assistance.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To cut this short, nothing between the 12th and the 15th so no 13th, no 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And why is that? It looks like it's a meticulously-kept book that has dates after July 15th, although admittedly it misses the whole period of August and goes into September from what I can gather and it has a period immediately before that discussing the 12th or the 11th, the 10th of July. Why do you think, sir, because it was your Zvornik Brigade does it not have any information in this book relating to the 13th and 14th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the records, I know that it was Sreten Milosevic who was the duty operations officer on the 13th. I don't know why he made no entries. I could only guess, and I wouldn't like to go there. Between the 14th and the 15th, it was Jokic. Why no entries, I don't know. Even if any entries had been made in relation to the 13th and the 14th, they would have been identical to the entries made in the regular log and the regular combat report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You don't want to speculate why they're not in there, we probably shouldn't speculate as to whether it would be identical or not. But in any event, let me just change the subject quickly just so we can have this for foundational purposes for tomorrow. We saw the tactical intercepts, which for the record is P2232 and I just wanted to know some code-names that were used in that tactical intercept. Can you tell me what your code-name was when you were using or being captured on these tactical intercepts. What was your code-name?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Ostojic. Just to address your first comment before you asked the question, it is not quite the same thing me not being able to guess why something wasn't recorded, but it's a matter of a totally different order of things if I assume why something was not recorded. If you compare the 15th, the war diary entry, the regular log book and the regular combat -- interim combat report, you will see a high degree of similarity. The overlap would probably amount to 100 percent. That is the reason for my previous statement, and now I think you can take it from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will and I shouldn't have remarked, and thank you for advising me accordingly. Now, on the tactical intercepts, we can pull them up but we don't have that much time, do you as you sit here remember the various people who were captured on -- who they were. They used code names. And first I want to know what your code-name was? For example they used Lovac, Lovac 1, Vuk, Ikar, Pavle?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The communications plan and the radio network that we used during the blockade of the 28th Division at Snagovo and Crni Vrh were both produced by Dragan Obrenovic, both the communications plan and the radio network had code-names being used for the units involved in these activities. I was not part of the communications plan, and you won't find my code-name there. My code-name was Palma, which coincided with the code-name of the Zvornik Brigade command. As for any other code-names being mentioned here and the ones you mentioned, I only know as much as provided in Dragan Obrenovic's explanations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who was Lovac 1?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned about that the same time as you, Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who was Lovac?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The radio communications centre of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who was Ikar?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that one. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who was Pavle?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about Pavle either.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who other than you talked to Semso Muminovic regarding the activities on July 16th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe before the 16th, it was Dusko Vukotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What was his code-name?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Vuk, V-u-k, I think that was the one he used most frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: A couple more questions, we'll get back to this tomorrow, specifically the tactical intercept. Do you know just in the last minute, there was some testimony, I know you've heard of it, I think you have, when they talk about the unofficial Zvornik Brigade operations duty officers' notebook or log book which is P377. Do you know who had possession of that immediately after the events of July 1995? Who took physical possession of it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for where this book went and who used it, I only heard here during some of the evidence that was given following the removal of the Zvornik Brigade all of the documents remained and nothing was removed at least for as long as I was still commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in 1999 when you met with Obrenovic on the one or two occasions, did he ever tell you that he had possession of these books at any time?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did he at any time tell you when you had your meeting in 1999 that he was writing in the book after the fact, post facto like the post facto construct that I talked about earlier. Did he ever tell you that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we met in Belgrade in 2000, but he never told me anything about this documentation or what was done with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that we could probably end today with the Court's permission. Thank you, Mr. Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, we'll continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: be reconvened on Friday, the 20th day of February, 2009 at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.00 p.m. to
